query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor Cr addition into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy (e.g., by partially substituting Ti or adding an extra 5–10 at.% Cr) will promote the in situ formation of a protective Cr‐Ta–rich oxide (such as a CrTaO4-based layer) during high-temperature exposure, thereby markedly improving oxygen resistance without compromising the beneficial room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength of the cast alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by a single intervention – addition of a modest amount of Cr (around 5–10 at.%), either by partial substitution of Ti or by overall alloying, to encourage selective oxidation.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures near 1000 °C for durations on the order of 50–200 hours; mechanical testing under similar high-temperature strain rate conditions (10−4–10−2 s−1) to verify yield strength retention; room temperature tensile property measurements to confirm ductility preservation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4-based oxide layer on the alloy surface, which acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: The added Cr alters the local oxidation kinetics at the surface by promoting selective oxidation that combines with Ta to form a stable, slow-growing CrTaO4-based scale. This layer reduces the outward diffusion of reactive metals and the inward diffusion of oxygen, thereby suppressing pest oxidation while maintaining the metallic microstructure responsible for mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Cr-modified alloy is predicted to show a significantly reduced mass gain during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (indicating slower oxidation kinetics) and diminished scale spallation, while retaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (ductility, yield strength, and oxidation resistance measured via weight gain and scale integrity) of the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature oxidation conditions (approximately 1000 °C in air, tested up to 200 hours) and under thermal-mechanical loading conditions similar to those originally reported for the equiatomic alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The evidence combining the beneficial role of Cr in forming a protective CrTaO4 layer in refractory alloys (PMC6513993, records 015 and 017) with oxidation studies on related Cr-containing RHEAs (PMC10142552, record 013) suggests that Cr addition could be effective in the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr system. However, the exact optimal Cr amount, its effect on phase stability, and any potential slight modifications of the mechanical behavior remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set with the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition and another with an added 5–10 at.% Cr (accomplished by partial replacement of Ti or via direct addition). Subject both to identical isothermal oxidation tests in air at 1000 °C for durations up to 200 hours. Perform complementary mechanical tests (room-temperature tensile testing and high-temperature yield strength tests under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1) on both sets.
measurements: Mass gain over time during oxidation (to determine oxidation kinetics) and scale integrity via microscopy (to assess spallation and oxide layer continuity).
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength measurements to check that mechanical performance is maintained.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (i.e., mass gain and spallation behavior) relative to the unmodified alloy, or if the mechanical properties (ductility and/or yield strength) are degraded beyond acceptable bounds compared with the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

When Cr is not added, the weight gain and oxidation rate of the WVTaTi high-entropy alloy coating oxide are 10.41 mg/cm2 and 0.21 mg/(cm2·h), respectively. With the increase in Cr content, the weight increases of oxide on the coating surface decreases. The addition of Cr resulted in the smallest increase in oxidation weight of the Cr1 RHEA coating, with a mass increase of 5.12 mg/cm2 and an oxidation rate of 0.10 mg/(cm2·h). According to the oxidation-resistance rating standard of steel, superalloy, and high-temperature protective coatings (HB5258-2000) [], it can be seen that Cr1 RHEA coating belongs to the antioxidant alloys, and Cr0.25, Cr0.5, and Cr0.75 belong to the sub-antioxidant alloys. In general, the proper addition of the Cr element can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the coating.
